\begin{abstract}
Speech recognition (ASR) systems are usually compared by word error rate (WER) on recorded files, after punctuation, capital letters and number format are removed. In dictation, the audio is streamed live and the text goes into the user's message as written, so what matters is which mistakes the user has to fix. We streamed 106 scripted English dictations from one speaker (read in a quiet room, with a fan on, and whispered), 20 clips in each of eleven other language and dialect sets, and 400 recordings that join clips in two languages to eleven ASR systems. We then sorted every error by a fixed rule into four levels: recognition, output formatting, language handling and, for the models we run ourselves, audio dropped before the model. Systems with similar WER failed in different ways. Zoom Scribe and OpenAI's GPT-Live-Transcribe have almost the same WER on quiet English (7.4\% and 7.3\%), but 34.7\% and 8.8\% on whispered English: Zoom and both AssemblyAI models left out 26--28\% of whispered words, and still 21--26\% with their end-of-turn detection relaxed or off, while seven other systems left out at most 3\%. Qwen3-ASR left out 32\%, but only because of the speech detection in our own deployment; relaxed, it left out 6\%. With 107 speakers from the EARS corpus, the same four systems again lost 7--31\% of whispered words, as did our self-hosted Whisper (10\%), while six others lost under 2\%. With only English selected, Gemini, Deepgram and our self-hosted Whisper lost the non-English part of a two-language recording in 86--99\% of recordings, against 33--46\% with both languages selected, while GPT-Live-Transcribe, OpenAI's realtime Whisper and Meta lost it in at most 20\%. Running Whisper behind the Silero voice activity detector, set to drop audio it judges to be silence, raised whispered WER from 10.1\% to 51.4\%. Most English results come from one read speaker. We release the code, the recordings, both references and every transcript.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
This paper studies one use of ASR systems, which we call \emph{dictation}: the user speaks a message, an email, a note or an instruction to an AI assistant, and the text is placed into another app. The transcript is the final product. Every error stays in the message unless the user finds it and corrects it, and correcting recognition errors is a large part of the cost of entering text by voice \citep{vertanen2010parakeet,ruan2017speech}.

WER counts errors but does not say what kind they are. On a dictation of eleven sentences of similar length, a WER of 9\% could mean one wrong word in every eleven, or one whole sentence missing from otherwise correct text. A single average can also hide large differences between groups of speakers \citep{koenecke2020racial} and between dialects \citep{talafha2024casablanca}.

Public benchmarks run complete audio files through each system and report WER on normalised text \citep{radford2023whisper,srivastav2026openasr}. Dictation differs in four ways that we test:
\begin{itemize}\itemsep0pt
  \item the audio is streamed, so we stream it at the speed of speech and measure how long the final text takes after the audio ends;
  \item the text is used as written, so we score numbers as written and also report errors in punctuation and capital letters;
  \item people dictate in different conditions, so we record English in a quiet room, with a fan on and in a whisper;
  \item people dictate in other languages and mix languages, so we test 11 language and dialect sets covering 7 languages, and recordings that switch from one language to another.
\end{itemize}

We test eleven systems: two open models that we run ourselves and nine services run by their providers. Every transcript is lined up with the correct text word by word, and each error is sorted by a fixed rule into one of four groups, which we call \emph{levels}: recognition, output formatting, language handling, and the audio path before the model (Section~\ref{sec:taxonomy}). The levels describe what the output shows, not a proven cause.

The main finding is that systems with similar WER fail in different ways, and that the differences are large. Zoom and GPT-Live have almost the same quiet-English WER (7.4\% and 7.3\%), but on whispered English Zoom leaves out 28\% of words and GPT-Live 1\%. With only English selected, some systems remove the other language of a two-language recording almost every time and others keep it. And the app around the model matters: running Whisper behind a voice activity detector that drops audio it judges to be silence raised its whispered WER from 10.1\% to 51.4\%.

The paper makes four contributions:
\begin{itemize}\itemsep0pt
  \item \textbf{A failure taxonomy for streaming dictation} that groups error types by the level they show up at, with a stated rule for detecting each type (Section~\ref{sec:taxonomy}).
  \item \textbf{A per-level comparison of eleven systems} on in-house data and on two external corpora with many speakers, including two behaviours known for open models \citep{peng2023prompting,rahman2026scriptcollapse,azeemi2026southasian} that, to our knowledge, have not been measured for commercial streaming systems: a language setting that removes the other language for some systems and only guides the language for others, and output in the wrong writing system (Sections~\ref{sec:overall}--\ref{sec:cs}).
  \item \textbf{Two references for the same speech}: the script the speaker meant (the \emph{script reference}) and a record of what they said (the \emph{spoken reference}), which separate a system that hears every word from one that writes the intended message (Section~\ref{sec:cleanup}).
  \item \textbf{A case study of the level before the model}: nine ways of running Whisper that differ in hosting, in how the audio is cut, in which voice activity detector (VAD) is used, and in whether the VAD drops audio before the model (Section~\ref{sec:whisperguide}).
\end{itemize}
We release the test client, the analysis code, the English recordings, both references and every system's transcripts.

\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related}
\paragraph{ASR benchmarks and error analysis.} Public leaderboards test open models and commercial services on complete audio files from public datasets, and clean up the text first so that differences in formatting do not count as errors \citep{srivastav2026openasr,radford2023whisper}. Independent tests of commercial services stream audio at the speed of speech and report speed alongside accuracy \citep{aa}. WER depends on how the text is normalised and on the test data \citep{szymanski2020wer}, and WER on one test set is a poor guide to WER on others \citep{likhomanenko2021rethinking}. Other measures look past WER: match error rate and word information lost \citep{morris2004wer}, semantic distance between reference and transcript \citep{kim2021semdist}, scores that split hallucinations by kind \citep{koudounas2026shallow}, and rates of runs of inserted or deleted words per hour \citep{ramirez2024anatomy}. Error analysis has shown which words are hard to recognise, such as rare words and words near disfluencies \citep{goldwater2010words}, and work on detecting and correcting ASR errors is reviewed by \citet{errattahi2018errors}. Error categories close to ours have been applied to Whisper on South Asian languages, where output in the wrong writing system caused most failures in three of four languages \citep{azeemi2026southasian}, and wrong-script output has been measured across many model--language pairs \citep{rahman2026scriptcollapse} and removed from WER by mapping both texts to one script \citep{pattnayak2026snwer}; these studies test open models. Some benchmarks score text closer to how it is written: ESB keeps casing and punctuation \citep{gandhi2022esb}, LibriSpeech-PC scores punctuation and capital letters \citep{meister2023librispeechpc}, and Earnings-21 reports accuracy on named entities \citep{delrio2021earnings21}. Most of these report how many errors a system makes on complete files. We report what kinds of errors commercial systems make in a streaming dictation setting, and we score the text as the user receives it, without converting numbers to a common form.

\paragraph{Dictation and text entry.} In a study of short messages on phones, speech entry was about three times faster than typing, with slightly more errors left in the final text \citep{ruan2017speech}; correcting recognition errors is a large part of the cost of speech entry \citep{vertanen2010parakeet}. This is why we care about which errors a user can see and fix.

\paragraph{Many languages and dialects.} FLEURS \citep{conneau2023fleurs} and VoxPopuli \citep{wang2021voxpopuli} provide read speech and parliament speeches in many languages. Arabic dialects remain much harder for current systems than Modern Standard Arabic \citep{talafha2024casablanca,alharbi2024sada}. Arabic dialects also have no standard spelling, which has led to spelling conventions \citep{habash2012coda} and to scoring against several correct texts \citep{ali2015multireference}. Urdu ASR has been benchmarked on read and conversational speech \citep{arif2025werwestand}. Urdu is also often written in Latin letters (Roman Urdu), and converting code-mixed Roman Urdu back to Urdu script is a task of its own \citep{wisal2022cmrutu}.

\paragraph{Switching languages.} Code-switching, moving between languages between or within sentences \citep{poplack1980sometimes}, has long been hard for speech and language technology \citep{winata2023decades}. Existing corpora, such as SEAME \citep{lyu2010seame} and ASCEND \citep{lovenia2022ascend} for Mandarin and English, contain natural switches within a sentence, for a few language pairs. For Whisper, the language given in the prompt changes code-switched output, and a single language can lead it to write a translation instead of a transcript \citep{peng2023prompting}. WER over a whole recording can hide errors on the switched words, which has led to scoring only those words \citep{ugan2025pier}. We instead build recordings that switch between sentences, for many language pairs. These recordings are less natural, but they reduce the chance that a language was lost because it is hard on its own.

\paragraph{Whispered speech.} Whispered speech has no voicing and is much harder for recognisers trained on normal speech \citep{lim2011whisper}; work on whispered ASR adapts models to it, for example with synthetic pseudo-whisper training data \citep{ghaffarzadegan2016whisper}. Corpora with whispered readings include wTIMIT \citep{lim2011whisper}, CHAINS \citep{cummins2006chains}, AISHELL6-Whisper for Mandarin \citep{li2026aishell6whisper} and EARS \citep{richter2024ears}, which records the same text read normally and whispered by 107 speakers; we use EARS to compare the systems across speakers.

Further related work, on latency, partial text, the written form and running Whisper, is in Appendix~\ref{app:related}.

\section{A Failure Taxonomy}\label{sec:taxonomy}
We group error types into four levels, by where in the pipeline the error shows up (Table~\ref{tab:taxonomy}).
\begin{itemize}\itemsep0pt
  \item \textbf{Recognition}: words missed, misheard or invented.
  \item \textbf{Output formatting}: words recognised but written in a form the user did not intend, such as a number in words instead of digits, or text in the wrong writing system. \emph{Inverse text normalisation} (ITN) is the step that turns spoken forms such as ``seven'' into written forms such as ``7''.
  \item \textbf{Language handling}: one language of a two-language message dropped, written in Latin letters, or translated.
  \item \textbf{Before the model}: audio the app never sends to the system.
\end{itemize}
The levels describe what we observe in the output, not a proven cause. For the hosted services, a missing word could have been lost in the service's own speech detection rather than in its model, and a language could be lost because of when the service finalises text rather than how it handles languages (Section~\ref{sec:cs}). We can separate the level before the model from recognition only for the models we run ourselves, Whisper and Qwen, whose audio path we control (Sections~\ref{sec:whisper} and~\ref{sec:whisperguide}). Every result therefore describes a system together with our integration of it (Appendix~\ref{app:systems}).

Each type has a stated rule that a program applies to the word-by-word comparison. Three rules rely on earlier judgements: which words are names was decided by a language model following a written rule; the spoken reference was corrected by one listener; and the rules for romanised and translated parts were checked by hand only on examples (Appendix~\ref{app:limits}).

\section{How We Ran the Test}\label{sec:setup}
\paragraph{Systems.} We test eleven systems that transcribe in real time. Two are open models that we run ourselves: Qwen3-ASR 1.7B \citep{qwen3asr} (``Qwen'') and Whisper Large V3 \citep{radford2023whisper} (``Whisper SH'', self-hosted). Nine are run by their providers: Meta Muse Voice Transcribe (``Meta''); Gemini 3.5 Transcribe (Live API; ``Gemini''); Deepgram Nova-3; AssemblyAI Universal-3.6 Pro and Universal-3.5 Pro (``AAI 3.6'' and ``AAI 3.5''); Zoom Scribe (Live API; ``Zoom''); ElevenLabs Scribe v2 Realtime (``ElevenLabs''); OpenAI GPT-Live-Transcribe (Realtime API; ``GPT-Live''); and OpenAI GPT-Realtime-Whisper, OpenAI's hosted streaming Whisper (``RT Whisper''). Section~\ref{sec:whisperguide} compares nine ways of running Whisper; the main comparison uses two of them, Whisper SH and RT Whisper. The main runs took place between 1 and 21 October 2026, the EARS and VOiCES runs and further Whisper and Gemini tests on 21--24 October, follow-up runs on 29 October, and on 5 November Qwen's two-language runs and the checks of GPT-Live's delay setting, of end-of-turn settings and of regional language codes (Appendix~\ref{app:systems}).

We use each system's default settings, with a few changes given in Appendix~\ref{app:systems}. Each system is told the language a user would choose, as a language code without a region unless a system needs one; if a system has no option for that language, we send none and the system detects the language itself. Sending each dialect's own regional code, where a provider documents one, changed almost nothing (Appendix~\ref{app:systems}).

\paragraph{Clean-up settings.} Gemini and ElevenLabs write every word as spoken by default, including fillers, repeats and false starts, and each offers a setting that removes them: Gemini's Smart mode, which also adds punctuation, capital letters and structured formatting \citep{geminitranscribedocs}, and ElevenLabs' \texttt{no\_verbatim} option \citep{elevenlabsdocs}. We report these as two extra rows, ``Gemini Smart'' and ``ElevenLabs NV'' (no verbatim), so the result tables have thirteen rows. Where we count errors that all systems share, we count the eleven systems and leave these two rows out.

\paragraph{In-house English.} 106 English messages, written by us to resemble chat, email, notes and prompts to AI assistants, were read aloud by one speaker, a member of our team, so the in-house English results describe one voice. Each message was recorded once, in one condition: 73 in a quiet room, 17 with a fan running nearby and 16 in a whisper. The three conditions use different messages, so we compare systems within a condition, not the conditions with each other; the fan-on set is a second set of read messages, not a test of noise. We call the third condition \emph{whispered speech}; the model is always named by its setup (for example Whisper SH), to keep the two apart. The reader deliberately moved between US, South Asian, British and Irish English, often within a message (Appendix~\ref{app:accent}).

\paragraph{Two references.} Each English message has two correct texts. The \emph{script reference} is the text the reader was given: what they meant to send. The \emph{spoken reference} is what they actually said, made by correcting the script against the audio. The two differ in 85 of the 106 messages, by 453 of 10{,}776 words (4.2\%): 242 added, 88 left out and 123 changed, including repeated words and spoken self-corrections. To make the spoken reference, a program proposed an edit wherever several systems heard the same departure from the script, and one listener accepted or rejected each proposal and corrected the rest by hand (Appendix~\ref{app:data}). Unless stated otherwise, English results use the script reference, because it is what a dictation user wants on the screen; Section~\ref{sec:cleanup} compares the two.

\paragraph{Other languages, two-language recordings and no-speech clips.} We take 20 short clips from each of 11 language and dialect sets in public datasets (Table~\ref{tab:data}). From these we build 400 recordings that join two clips in different languages (Section~\ref{sec:cs}). We also include 10 clips with no speech (silence and background noise) to check whether a system writes text when nobody is speaking. The single-language clips add up to 99 minutes of speech.

\paragraph{External corpora.} Two public corpora with many speakers repeat the whispering and noise tests: EARS and VOiCES (Sections~\ref{sec:whisper} and~\ref{sec:voices}, Appendix~\ref{app:ext}). We keep them apart from our own data and score them differently.

\paragraph{Sending the audio.} Each clip is streamed at the speed of speech in small chunks, the way a microphone delivers it, with a new session for every clip and all systems called from the same client machine (Appendix~\ref{app:systems}). A system \emph{finalises} text when it commits to it and stops revising it; we score only finalised text.

A voice activity detector (VAD) is a small model that decides whether audio contains speech. Except where Section~\ref{sec:whisperguide} says otherwise, no VAD drops any audio: every system receives every sample. Whisper SH uses Silero VAD \citep{silero} only to decide where to cut the audio into segments. Section~\ref{sec:whisperguide} measures what happens when a VAD also drops audio, using a second Whisper deployment of ours with a VAD in front of it on the client (``gated Whisper'').

\paragraph{Scoring.} Before comparing a transcript with the correct text, we ignore capital letters and punctuation, and we treat variant letter forms in Arabic, Urdu and Chinese as equal (Appendix~\ref{app:data}). We do not convert numbers: we score the text as written, so ``seven'' in place of ``7'' counts as an error.

Each transcript is lined up with the correct text (the reference) using the fewest possible edits (a Levenshtein alignment). This gives three kinds of word error: a \emph{substitution} (a wrong word), a \emph{deletion} (a missing word) and an \emph{insertion} (an extra word). WER is the total number of errors in a set divided by the total number of words in its correct text. It can exceed 100\%, because extra words also count as errors. Mandarin, which is not written with spaces, is scored by counting each Chinese character as one unit (Appendix~\ref{app:data}). The \emph{character error rate} (CER) is the same measure counted over characters. We also report a \emph{formatted} error rate, a case- and punctuation-sensitive WER as in ESB \citep{gandhi2022esb}: words keep their capital letters and each punctuation mark counts as a separate token, so a wrong capital or a missing comma each counts as one error.

\paragraph{Uncertainty.} For English WER we give a 95\% confidence interval from a percentile bootstrap over clips with 2{,}000 resamples \citep{bisani2004bootstrap} (4{,}000 for the significance tests). These intervals describe variation across messages, not across speakers. When we compare two systems, or one system under two conditions, we resample the same clips for both (a paired comparison). A difference is \emph{clear} when the 95\% interval of the paired difference excludes zero and it still holds after a Holm correction for the number of comparisons in its group (for example, the 13 name gaps form one group; Appendix~\ref{app:data}); otherwise it is \emph{within chance}. The language sets have only 20 clips each, so differences of a few points there are within chance. Differences are given in percentage points (``points'').

\section{One Score, Different Failures}\label{sec:overall}
\paragraph{Similar WER on quiet English, different WER elsewhere.} Table~\ref{tab:overall} gives each system's WER and formatted error rate for each English condition. On quiet English, ten of the thirteen rows are between 3.9\% and 9.5\%, and the order of these systems tells little about the other conditions. Zoom (7.4\%) and GPT-Live (7.3\%) are the clearest case: on whispered English, Zoom's WER is 34.7\% and GPT-Live's 8.8\% (paired difference 25.8 points, 95\% CI 10.3 to 51.7), almost all of it missing words. AAI 3.6 (8.2\%) and RT Whisper (8.2\%) are another: 30.5\% and 8.9\% whispered. Gemini Smart has the lowest quiet-English WER (3.9\%), clearly below the next row, ElevenLabs NV; the lowest with default settings is Gemini, at 6.9\%. When capital letters and punctuation are also scored, error rates on quiet English rise to 8.8--22.8\%; Gemini Smart (8.8\%), ElevenLabs NV (9.0\%) and Gemini (9.1\%) are lowest.

\paragraph{Other languages.} For European languages and Mandarin the systems are close, and most stay below 10\%. Hindi ranges from 2.6\% to 34.6\%, Urdu is above 85\% for several systems (Section~\ref{sec:script}), and the Saudi and Emirati Arabic sets are hard for every system (Section~\ref{sec:dialects}). No system is clearly best on any language set. Appendix~\ref{app:extra} gives WER for each set (Table~\ref{tab:overalllang}).

\paragraph{Speed.} Measured from our test client, typical (median) waits from the end of the audio to the final text range from 313 to 760\,ms. Meta, Deepgram, Whisper SH, Qwen and both ElevenLabs settings wait under 400\,ms; GPT-Live and RT Whisper about 750\,ms. Appendix~\ref{app:speed} gives the full timings, which we treat as indicative.

\section{Recognition}\label{sec:recognition}
\subsection{Wrong, Missing and Extra Words}\label{sec:mix}
WER adds three kinds of error together: wrong words (substitutions), missing words (deletions) and extra words (insertions). Table~\ref{tab:fmix} splits each system's WER into these three parts for quiet English, English with the fan on, and the other languages.

\paragraph{Quiet English.} Against the script reference, extra words are the largest part of the error for nine of the thirteen rows: Gemini, for example, has 3.7\% extra words against 2.1\% wrong ones, and ElevenLabs 8.1\% against 2.8\%. Many of these extra words were really said: they are repeats and self-corrections the reader added. Against the spoken reference, extra words are the largest part for only four rows (Gemini, AAI 3.5, Zoom and ElevenLabs): Gemini's extra words fall from 3.7\% to 1.6\%, but ElevenLabs' only to 5.7\%, so most of ElevenLabs' extra words were not said. The mix also differs between systems with the same WER: Whisper SH and AAI 3.6 (8.3\% and 8.2\%) differ by only 0.1 points in WER, but Whisper SH misses more words (by 0.9 points, 95\% CI 0.1 to 2.4) and adds fewer (by 1.1 points, 95\% CI 0.5 to 1.8). Missing words are between 1.1\% and 2.7\% for every system.

\paragraph{With a fan on and in other languages.} On the fan-on set, wrong words are the largest part for all thirteen rows; Deepgram has the most, 7.0\%. Outside English, wrong words are also the largest part for every system: 7.6--13.1\% of words, against 1.9--5.7\% missing and 0.5--1.2\% extra.

\paragraph{What the wrong words are.} For every system, ordinary words are the largest group of wrong English words (46--63\%). Numbers written as words instead of digits or the other way round (Section~\ref{sec:numbers}), and near-misses such as ``request'' for ``requests'', together make up 33--50\%; names are 3--5\% (Appendix~\ref{app:extra}, Table~\ref{tab:fsubkind}).

\subsection{Whispered Speech}\label{sec:whisper}
\paragraph{Four systems leave out whispered words.} On whispered speech, Qwen, Zoom and both AAI models leave out 26--32\% of words; every other row leaves out at most 3\% (Figure~\ref{fig:whispermix}). With 16 clips these shares are uncertain (for Qwen, 95\% CI 15--58\%), but each of the four intervals lies above 3\% (this also holds with bias-corrected intervals and after a Holm correction). Their errors are concentrated in some clips: 5 or 6 of the 16 whispered clips fail (WER of 50\% or more), and 2--4 are almost entirely lost (90\% or more). In the other group, no whispered clip fails, and wrong words are the largest part of the error for every row except Gemini Smart, whose few errors are split about evenly between wrong and missing words.

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\tabinput tables/fig_whispermix.tex
\caption{Whispered WER split into wrong, missing and extra words, as a share of all words; the number is the WER. Four systems lose most of their whispered words as missing words; the rest mostly get words wrong.}
\label{fig:whispermix}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Where the words go missing.} Both AAI models cut off the last 3 or more words of 4 of the 16 whispered clips. Qwen's missing stretches appear anywhere, including at the start. A cut-off ending leaves no visible gap in the text, and WER does not show it: AAI 3.6 (30.5\%) and Zoom (34.7\%) have similar whispered WER, but 4 of AAI 3.6's whispered clips have a cut-off ending and none of Zoom's (too few clips to test).

\paragraph{Recognition, turn detection or speech detection?} Qwen, Zoom and the AAI models all decide on the server when speech or a turn has ended, so a missing whispered word could be lost there rather than in recognition. On 5 November we tested this on the 16 whispered clips (Appendix~\ref{app:systems}). For AAI, forcing the end of the last turn before closing the session changed nothing (AAI 3.6: 25.7\% of words missing, then 25.6\%), and turning end-of-turn detection off (\texttt{end\_of\_turn\_confidence\_threshold} 1, 10\,s maximum silence) left 22.7\% missing for AAI 3.6 and 25.7\% for AAI 3.5. For Zoom, ending a segment after 5\,s of silence instead of 600\,ms lowered missing words from 27.6\% to 21.2\%. So AAI and, for the most part, Zoom lose these words whatever their turn settings; since we cannot see inside a hosted service, we count this as recognition, which here includes any speech detection inside the service. Qwen is different: our deployment runs its own speech detection before the model, with default settings, and relaxing it (threshold 0.3, 2\,s of silence) lowered Qwen's missing words from 32.2\% to 5.7\%. Qwen's whispered loss is therefore in the audio path of our own deployment, the level before the model, as for gated Whisper (Section~\ref{sec:whisperguide}). The relaxed setting cost nothing we could measure: on the 46 quiet and 14 fan-on messages that completed (the longest timed out on our single server), WER was 10.3\% against 11.3\% and 5.6\% against 6.3\% with the default, and it wrote no text on the 10 no-speech clips. The tables keep the deployment's default setting.

\paragraph{The same pattern across 107 speakers.} EARS \citep{richter2024ears} has 107 speakers recorded in a sound-proofed studio, reading the same passage (the Rainbow Passage) normally and in a whisper; we use parts 1--4 from every speaker, 428 normal and 428 whispered clips. For EARS we normalise numbers and spellings in reference and transcript with Whisper's English text normaliser and report only WER; intervals resample speakers. Table~\ref{tab:ears} gives the results. Normal speech is easy for every system here (0.8--2.5\%). Every speaker reads the same well-known passage, which a system may have seen in training; we cannot check this, so EARS tests the same text across many voices, not unseen text. Whispered, the same four systems again lose words, now 7--31\% of them: AAI 3.6 and AAI 3.5 rise by about 7 points, Zoom by 24 and Qwen by 31 (with its deployment's default speech detection, as in the tables). Whisper SH, which lost few words on our whispered clips, loses 10.4\% of words as missing on EARS, against 7.3\% for each AAI model (within chance), so the two groups of our in-house test are not a clean split across speakers. Gemini (in both settings), ElevenLabs (in both settings), Meta, GPT-Live and RT Whisper change by less than one point, and no speaker reaches a whispered WER of 20\% with any of them.

\subsection{Names}\label{sec:names}
\paragraph{Names are written correctly less often than other words.} Our English scripts name people, products and apps (for example, ``send it to Maria'' or ``post it in Notion''). Over all English dictation, every system writes names correctly less often than other words (Table~\ref{tab:fnames}). Deepgram, used without its custom-vocabulary option, has the largest gap: 9.7 points (95\% CI 3.3 to 16.7). Five more systems have gaps of 4.8--6.5 points with intervals that exclude zero, but these are 13 comparisons, and after a Holm correction only Deepgram's gap remains clear. Names are 183 of 10{,}776 words, so even Deepgram's gap adds only about 0.2 points to its WER: a system can write many names wrongly and still have a low WER. Much of the gap comes from fan-on and whispered messages: on quiet English alone (123 name words), no system's gap is clearly above zero (Deepgram's is the largest, 6.4 points, 95\% CI $-0.4$ to 14.7), and Whisper SH's and Qwen's fall from 6.5 to under 2 points.

\paragraph{Finding the names.} We took every word in the English scripts that starts with a capital letter in the middle of a sentence: 327 words, 184 different ones. Each different word was labelled as a name or not by a written rule (Appendix~\ref{app:data}); only 156 of the 327 are names, so the capital-letter rule alone finds names poorly. The 183 name words we score are these 156, the 22 occurrences of a listed name at the start of a sentence or after a title such as ``Dr.'', and 5 lower-case uses of a word that names a product in the same message (such as ``app''), which our counting also includes.

\subsection{Dialects and Errors Every System Shares}\label{sec:dialects}
\paragraph{Most failed clips are in four sets.} In the eleven other language sets, WER is below 5\% on several European sets and near or above 50\% on Emirati Arabic and, for some systems, Urdu. Almost all failed clips are in four sets: Saudi Arabic, Emirati Arabic, Hindi and Urdu (Appendix~\ref{app:extra}, Table~\ref{tab:fworst}). Urdu and Hindi are about writing (Section~\ref{sec:script}); the Arabic dialects are about recognition.

\paragraph{Arabic dialects.} Saudi and Emirati Arabic have failed clips for every one of the eleven systems: 15--35\% and 50--75\% of clips. On Emirati Arabic, WER is between 48.8\% and 61.8\% with default settings. Part of the error may come from the correct text itself: Arabic dialects have no standard spelling \citep{habash2012coda}, so a correct transcript can be spelled differently from ours. Each dialect also comes from a single corpus, so we cannot separate the dialect from how its corpus was recorded.

\paragraph{Errors every system makes.} If every system fails on a clip, switching systems will not help; if only one fails, another system avoids it. Of the 220 non-English clips, 21 are hard clips (WER above 30\%) for all eleven systems: 14 Emirati Arabic, 6 Saudi Arabic and 1 Spanish (Spain). Across all 326 speech clips, 23 are hard for exactly one system (Appendix~\ref{app:extra}). In English, 67 of 73 quiet clips and all 17 fan-on clips are below 30\% for every system, while 13 of 16 whispered clips are above it for at least one: for English, the choice of system matters most on whispered speech.

\subsection{Distance and Noise}\label{sec:voices}
\paragraph{A far microphone, babble and a television.} VOiCES \citep{richey2018voices} replays audiobook sentences in a room and records them with a far microphone, in quiet, with several people talking (babble) and with a television playing. With babble, WER rises for every system, to between 38.7\% and 94.9\%, mostly as missing words; Zoom is lowest with babble and with television, although it is worse than average with a far microphone in a quiet room. Gemini returned no text within 30 seconds on 67 of the 100 babble clips, which count as empty transcripts; on the other 33 its WER is 40.3\%, so most of its babble WER is a failure to answer rather than misrecognition. Appendix~\ref{app:ext} gives the full results.

\section{Output Formatting}\label{sec:formatting}
\subsection{Number Format}\label{sec:numbers}
\paragraph{Each system has its own habit.} Most benchmarks convert numbers to a common form before scoring; we do not, so we can see how each system's ITN writes them. The English scripts contain 276 numbers written in digits and 193 written as words (such as ``first'' or ``twenty''). Qwen writes 68\% of the digit numbers as words (``seven'' for ``7''), Meta 47\% and GPT-Live 45\%; the two AAI models do the opposite, turning 41--42\% of number words into digits; Whisper SH, Gemini, Zoom and ElevenLabs usually keep the form in the script (Appendix~\ref{app:extra}, Table~\ref{tab:fnumbers}). These switches make up 16.1\% of GPT-Live's English errors, 12.9\% of Meta's and 10.4\% of Qwen's, against 4.8--6.1\% for ElevenLabs, Zoom and Whisper SH; a number written in several words counts once, so these shares are a minimum. The number itself was heard correctly.

\paragraph{The order of systems barely changes.} Re-scored after Whisper's English text normaliser, which writes numbers as digits and removes fillers, every quiet-English WER falls, by 1.0--3.8 points when both scores use the same word splitting, but the order of systems changes little (rank correlation 0.98; Appendix~\ref{app:extra}, Table~\ref{tab:normwer}). Number habits matter to a user who sees the text, but they are not what separates the systems on quiet English.

\subsection{Writing System}\label{sec:script}
\paragraph{Urdu.} Urdu shows the biggest gap between systems, and the cause is mostly the writing system. Table~\ref{tab:urdu} counts, for each system that writes Urdu in another script, the clips written mostly in Devanagari, the script of Hindi. Qwen, Meta and AAI 3.5 write most Urdu clips in Devanagari and fail on 85--95\% of them. Meta and AAI 3.5 have no Urdu option and detect the language themselves; Qwen does this even when Urdu is selected. Spoken Urdu and Hindi are close, so a system detecting the language itself may reasonably hear Hindi; but a user who chose Urdu receives text in the wrong writing system, whatever words it contains. Zoom, which also has no Urdu option, writes 19 of 20 Urdu clips in Latin letters (``Ek bum governoral journal ke daftar\ldots'') and fails on every one. Both Whisper rows, Deepgram, AAI 3.6 and ElevenLabs write in the Urdu writing system and fail on at most 5\% of clips; RT Whisper has the lowest Urdu WER (12.3\%).

\paragraph{Hindi.} Zoom has the highest Hindi WER of the eleven systems (34.6\%), with text in the right writing system. Its CER (16.3\%) is less than half its WER, so many of its wrong words differ from the correct word by a few characters, for example in vowel signs, rather than being different words (Appendix~\ref{app:extra}).

\subsection{Clean-up and the Two References}\label{sec:cleanup}
\paragraph{The reference decides which system looks best.} The script reference asks whether the text is the message the user meant; the spoken reference asks whether the system heard what was said. A clean-up setting removes fillers, repeats and self-corrections on purpose, so it scores well on the first and loses points on the second. In the literature this is disfluency removal, and the choice between verbatim and clean transcripts \citep{jamshidlou2020disfluency}.

\paragraph{Against the script.} Smart lowers Gemini's quiet-English WER from 6.9\% to 3.9\%, and \texttt{no\_verbatim} lowers ElevenLabs' from 12.8\% to 5.1\%, in both cases almost all through fewer extra words.

\paragraph{Against what was said.} Table~\ref{tab:verbatim} scores the same transcripts against the spoken reference. Every system run at its verbatim default does better on quiet English, by 2.2--4.0 points, because words the reader added are no longer counted as extra. Gemini Smart is the only row that does worse (+0.8 points, paired 95\% CI $-0.1$ to 1.6): it leaves out the repeats and self-corrections that are now in the reference. On quiet English, Gemini (3.7\%), ElevenLabs NV (4.5\%) and Gemini Smart (4.6\%) are now close. In paired comparisons, Gemini is 0.9 points below Gemini Smart (95\% CI $-1.8$ to 0.0), and Gemini Smart and ElevenLabs NV are 0.1 points apart. Against the script, Gemini Smart is clearly below ElevenLabs NV (by 1.2 points, 95\% CI 0.6 to 1.9); against what was said, no clean-up setting is clearly ahead. The whispered results of Section~\ref{sec:whisper} hold against either reference: every whispered WER moves by at most 1.5 points.

\paragraph{How much the spoken reference depends on the systems.} The spoken reference was drafted from where the verbatim systems agreed, so it could favour them. Each system voted for 237 to 313 of the 378 accepted edits. We rebuilt the reference eleven times, each time keeping only the accepted edits that the other ten systems would still have proposed: no system's WER against its own rebuilt reference rose by more than 0.3 points in any condition (1.2 points for Meta on quiet English with the stricter thresholds used to pre-tick proposals). But the order of Gemini, Gemini Smart and ElevenLabs NV is not stable: without Gemini's votes, Gemini is 0.5 points below Gemini Smart (95\% CI $-1.3$ to 0.3), and with the stricter pre-tick thresholds, it is 0.8 points above (95\% CI $-0.1$ to 1.7); neither difference is clear. A clean-up setting is clearly best only against the script.

\section{Language Handling: Two Languages in One Recording}\label{sec:cs}
\paragraph{With only English selected, some systems remove the other language.} We call the English-only setting a \emph{filter} for a system when, with only English selected, the other language is lost in more than half of the EN\,+\,X recordings, against fewer than half with both languages selected; and a \emph{preference} when, with only English selected, it is lost in fewer than half. By this rule, the setting is a filter for Gemini (in both settings), Deepgram and Whisper SH: the non-English part is lost in 86--99\% of the 100 recordings with only English selected, against 33--46\% with both selected (Table~\ref{tab:fcs}, first column; Table~\ref{tab:csoverall} counts a loss of either part). It is a preference for Qwen, Meta, AAI 3.6, AAI 3.5, GPT-Live and RT Whisper, which lose it in 7--38\%. Zoom and ElevenLabs (in both settings) lose most second languages whatever is selected, for reasons given below. Whether a filter is right depends on the app; a user who selects English and then says a sentence in another language may or may not want it written.

\paragraph{How the recordings were built.} Our recordings are not natural code-switching \citep{poplack1980sometimes,winata2023decades}: they join single-language recordings from different speakers, with a 300\,ms pause between them, so the language, the speaker and the recording all change at a sentence boundary. 100 recordings pair English with one of the 10 other language sets (EN\,+\,X), and 300 pair two non-English languages (X\,+\,Y). Urdu is left out because several systems write it in the wrong writing system even alone (Section~\ref{sec:script}). English comes first in half of the EN\,+\,X recordings, and the order of each X\,+\,Y pair is balanced likewise. Each recording is played with both languages selected and with automatic detection, and EN\,+\,X recordings also with only English selected. All eleven systems were run on this test.

To score a recording, we line up the transcript with the two parts' correct texts joined end to end, and mark each reference word as heard, replaced or missing. A part is \emph{missing} when less than 20\% of its words are heard: either nothing is written in its place, or other text is. Table~\ref{tab:csoverall} gives the share of recordings in which a part goes missing. A part may also go missing because it is hard on its own; Appendix~\ref{app:cs} repeats the analysis on the 85 EN\,+\,X and 232 X\,+\,Y recordings whose parts every one of the eleven systems gets at least 50\% right when played alone (the \emph{screened} recordings); the order of the systems is almost the same and the conclusions do not change.

\paragraph{Which part goes missing.} Table~\ref{tab:fcs} (Appendix~\ref{app:cs}) shows which part goes missing and what appears in its place. Meta never loses the first part, in any setting; all of its losses are the second part. Gemini does the opposite: with automatic detection, it loses the first part in 54\% of EN\,+\,X recordings and the second in 19\%, and the lost part is the English one in 37 of the 100. GPT-Live loses a part in 6--7\% of EN\,+\,X recordings, almost always the second. Qwen also loses the second part more often than the first (14\% against 6\% of EN\,+\,X recordings with both languages selected, and 101 against 37 of the 300 X\,+\,Y); in 14 of its 20 EN\,+\,X losses it writes other text in the lost part's place. Whisper SH usually leaves a gap: with both languages selected, it loses the first part in 25\% of recordings and the second in 20\%, and in 43\% nothing is written where the part should be.

\paragraph{Romanised and translated parts leave no gap.} Deepgram rarely leaves a gap. Instead, in 34\% of the 50 EN\,+\,X recordings whose other language has its own writing system (Arabic, Hindi or Mandarin), it writes that part in Latin letters, mostly Arabic and Mandarin parts as strings of similar-sounding Latin syllables. Gemini, with both languages selected, writes the Hindi part in Latin letters in 5 of the 10 recordings of English and Hindi. A real English translation is mainly a Whisper behaviour, as reported for code-switched speech \citep{peng2023prompting}: Whisper SH, with only English selected, translates the other part into English in 18\% of these recordings. A check for missing text does not find romanised or translated parts.

\paragraph{One language per session, and finalising once.} Zoom took one language per session, so all three settings behave like English only: it loses a language in 62\% of EN\,+\,X recordings and 85\% of X\,+\,Y. Its Arabic, Hindi and Mandarin parts are lost in every recording, while most Spanish, German and French parts survive (43 of 130, 7 of 110 and 19 of 110 lost, with both languages selected). ElevenLabs, by default, finalises the whole recording as one block of text. It loses a part in 62\% of EN\,+\,X recordings (almost always the non-English part) and 93\% of X\,+\,Y; ElevenLabs NV in 80\% and 96\%. Set to finalise at each pause of 300\,ms, ElevenLabs lost a part in 1\% of the screened EN\,+\,X recordings and 36\% of the screened X\,+\,Y (Appendix~\ref{app:cs}). This pause matches the one we put between the two clips, so it favours this setting.

\section{Before the Model: A Case Study of Running Whisper}\label{sec:whisperguide}
Whisper is a widely used open ASR model. Unlike the hosted services in this paper, it leaves several choices to whoever runs it: where it is hosted, how the audio is cut into segments, and whether a VAD drops audio before the model hears it. On whispered speech, these choices changed our results more than the choice between most systems did. This section describes what we tried and what each choice did in our test.

\paragraph{The nine setups.} Table~\ref{tab:setups} lists them. Setups 1--6 run Whisper Large V3 on two deployments of ours. OpenAI does not say which Whisper version it serves for setups 7--9; at its 2023 launch it described its Whisper API model as Large V2 \citep{openaiwhisperapi}, so differences between setups 1--6 and 7--9 may come from the model version as well as from how it is run. Appendix~\ref{app:whisper} gives the exact rules of each setup.

\paragraph{Finding 1: Silero VAD dropping audio lost whispered speech.} With its VAD on, the gated deployment has a whispered WER of 80.7\%, and the VAD never sent 2 of the 16 whispered clips. Turning the VAD off lowers whispered WER by 19.6 points (95\% CI 7.0 to 36.9) and changes quiet and fan-on English by less than a point (Appendix~\ref{app:whisper}, Table~\ref{tab:vad}). The self-hosted deployment shows the same effect from the other side: sent all of the audio, its whispered WER is 10.1\%; with Silero dropping audio, 51.4\%, with 44.6\% of words missing. Both effects hold across the 107 EARS speakers: turning the gated deployment's VAD off lowers whispered WER by 10.1 points (95\% CI 8.0 to 12.2), and Silero dropping audio raises the self-hosted deployment's by 26.8 points (95\% CI 21.3 to 32.2), with 62 of the 107 speakers at 20\% or more, against 20 (Table~\ref{tab:earsvad}).

\paragraph{Finding 2: TEN VAD dropped audio with a much smaller loss.} When the VAD only cuts the audio, Silero and TEN give nearly the same results (whispered 10.1\% and 10.2\%). When it also drops audio, they differ sharply: with Silero, whispered WER rises to 51.4\%; with TEN, it stays at 10.7\%. On EARS, dropping with Silero gives 38.3\% and dropping with TEN 14.4\%, against 11.5\% for sending all of the audio; TEN's rise of 2.9 points is within chance (95\% CI $-0.4$ to 6.7). TEN keeps whispered speech because it calls most of it speech: 79\% of whispered 32\,ms windows at its default threshold, against 37\% for Silero. TEN does not do this by calling everything speech: on fan noise, steady noise, mains hum and television it calls about as much audio speech as Silero, and at most 2.2\% of the windows of any no-speech clip. It does call much more background talk speech: with babble, 97\% of windows against 80\% for Silero, 15 points more than on the same recordings without babble. We did not test what Whisper writes when TEN passes that audio.

\paragraph{Finding 3: lowering Silero's threshold did not fix it.} With Silero's drop threshold lowered from 0.5 to 0.2, whispered WER still stayed at 41.1\%, four times the 10.1\% of sending all of the audio, because even at 0.2 Silero calls only 52\% of the whispered audio speech (Appendix~\ref{app:whisper}, Figure~\ref{fig:vadsweep}). TEN keeps whispered WER between 10.0\% and 10.7\% at every threshold tried.

\paragraph{Finding 4: Whisper wrote invented text on silence.} Whisper can write text that was never said (hallucination) \citep{koenecke2024careless,mansoor2025mitigating}. On all 10 no-speech clips Whisper-1 wrote text, mostly ``you'' and ``Thank you for watching.'', and the self-hosted deployment wrote a stray ``.'' or ``so'' on 6 of 10. On two short Spanish (Spain) clips the self-hosted deployment replaced the whole speech with a stock phrase such as ``Muchas gracias.'' Dropping audio with a VAD removes text on silence, at the cost above.

\paragraph{Finding 5: the most accurate setups were the slowest.} Whisper-1, which transcribes the whole recording after the user stops, has the lowest quiet and whispered English WER of the nine setups (5.5\% and 7.7\%), but a typical wait of 1{,}850\,ms and text on every no-speech clip. RT Whisper is the most accurate on the other languages (14.0\% average, against 17.3--18.9\%) and loses a language in 11\% of two-language recordings, but accepts only one language and waits about twice as long as the self-hosted deployment (735\,ms against 361\,ms typical).

\paragraph{Finding 6: cutting at the speaker's pauses kept whispered words.} With its VAD off, the gated deployment still has a whispered WER of 61.1\%, almost all of it missing words, while the self-hosted deployment, which transcribes exactly the segments the client cuts at pauses, loses 1.8\% of whispered words on the same clips and 10.4\% on EARS. The two are different deployments, and the gated server runs its own speech detection, so this comparison does not isolate how the audio is cut (Appendix~\ref{app:whisper}).

\section{Recommendations for Testing ASR for Dictation}\label{sec:guidance}
Systems with similar error rates made different kinds of errors in our test, at every level of the taxonomy. We recommend that tests of ASR systems for dictation include the following.
\begin{itemize}\itemsep1pt
  \item \textbf{Recognition: report wrong, missing and extra words separately}, with missing stretches and cut-off endings, because a cut-off ending leaves no visible gap (Sections~\ref{sec:mix} and~\ref{sec:whisper}). Test whispered speech with several speakers. Report accuracy on names separately, because a gap of 1 point and one of 10 look almost the same in overall WER, and check which words are names (Section~\ref{sec:names}).
  \item \textbf{Output formatting: say which reference is used}, and score against both what the speaker meant and what they said when clean-up settings are compared (Section~\ref{sec:cleanup}). Check how numbers are written (Section~\ref{sec:numbers}) and the writing system of the output, especially for languages written in more than one (Section~\ref{sec:script}).
  \item \textbf{Language handling: test two-language speech under each language setting}, and tell missing, romanised and translated parts apart (Section~\ref{sec:cs}). Settings that seem unrelated to language can matter: ElevenLabs lost far fewer languages when it finalised text at each pause.
  \item \textbf{Before the model: test the whole app}, including any VAD and how the audio is cut, on whispered speech and on silence (Section~\ref{sec:whisperguide}).
  \item \textbf{Separate errors all systems share from errors one system makes.} Errors every system makes, such as on Saudi and Emirati Arabic, will not be fixed by switching among the tested systems (Section~\ref{sec:dialects}).
\end{itemize}

\section{Limitations}\label{sec:limits}
\begin{itemize}\itemsep1pt
  \item \textbf{One speaker.} The in-house English is 106 scripted messages read by one speaker, who varies accent deliberately but has one voice. It is read speech, not spontaneous dictation, so it has fewer and different disfluencies than real dictation, which matters most for the clean-up results.
  \item \textbf{Small sets.} There are 16 whispered messages and 20 clips per language set, so many counts are small and the tables show patterns rather than exact rates. Each message was recorded in only one condition, so the quiet, fan-on and whispered sets differ in their messages as well as their condition.
  \item \textbf{Corpora and sources.} Each dialect set comes from a single corpus, so dialect and recording source cannot be separated. The external corpora are read speech too, and their texts are public (EARS uses one well-known passage, VOiCES uses LibriSpeech \citep{panayotov2015librispeech}), so a system may have seen them in training; we cannot check this, and it could flatter their clean scores and make the whispered EARS test easier for systems that remember the passage.
  \item \textbf{Streaming.} We stream the audio and measure the wait for the final text, but we score only finalised text: we do not measure partial text or how it changes \citep{shangguan2020stability}, or how well a system decides by itself that the speaker has stopped.
  \item \textbf{Hosted systems change.} Results for hosted services reflect their versions in October 2026, tested on different days, and each clip was played once per system and setting except where stated.
\end{itemize}
Appendix~\ref{app:limits} lists further limitations: how the references and labels were made, choices made on the test data, systems and settings not fully tested, and timing.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}
We streamed the same audio to eleven ASR systems and grouped every error by the level it shows up at. Systems with similar error rates failed differently at each level. In recognition, three systems left out about a quarter of whispered words that the others heard, whatever their end-of-turn settings, a pattern that largely held across 107 external speakers, and names were written correctly less often than other words, by up to 9.7 points, though only Deepgram's gap is clear after correcting for the number of comparisons. In output formatting, systems differed in how they wrote numbers and in which writing system, and a clean-up setting wrote the message meant rather than every word said. In language handling, selecting only English removed the other language for some systems and not for others. Before the model, Silero VAD dropping audio raised Whisper's whispered WER from 10.1\% to 51.4\%, while TEN VAD did not clearly raise it, and the default speech detection of our Qwen deployment cost it most of its whispered words. Some errors, such as those on Saudi and Emirati Arabic, are made by every system. We recommend reporting these error types alongside WER and testing the app's whole audio path.

\section*{Ethics}
The English dictations were recorded by one member of our team, who volunteered to read scripted messages for this study and gave consent to the use of their recordings for it and to their public release; the consent is kept on record by the authors. The scripts were written for the study, and the people they name are invented, except that three email scripts are signed with the name of one of the authors, who agreed to this; the scripts contain no other personal data. No audio or text from users of any product is included. Because the test streams audio to hosted ASR services, the recordings were processed by those providers under their terms of service. The public clips are used under their licences. EARS (CC BY-NC 4.0) and VOiCES (CC BY 4.0) are used for non-commercial research evaluation only, kept apart from our own recordings and not redistributed. No data from this study, and no transcript returned by a tested system, was used to train any model; the systems' transcripts were used only to score them and to draft the spoken references (Section~\ref{sec:setup}).

\paragraph{Code and data availability.} The test client, the scoring and analysis code, and the scripts that build every table in this paper are released at \url{https://github.com/heylemon-ai/streaming-dictation-asr} under the Apache 2.0 licence. The in-house English recordings (quiet, fan on and whispered, and the no-speech clips), both references for each, and every tested system's transcripts are released at \url{https://huggingface.co/datasets/hey-lemon/streaming-dictation-asr} under CC BY 4.0. The other language sets, the two-language recordings, EARS and VOiCES are not redistributed. The dataset lists the public clips used and the recipe for the two-language recordings; the repository has scripts that fetch EARS and VOiCES from their sources and rebuild the two-language recordings once the public clips are in place.

\paragraph{Competing interests.} The authors work at a company that makes dictation software and is developing its own ASR model, and that has commercial relationships with some of the tested providers. The authors and their company have no partnership with any of the tested providers. This work received no external funding: it was carried out and paid for by the authors' company, and no tested provider funded it.

\section{Further Related Work}\label{app:related}
\paragraph{Latency and the written form.} In streaming ASR, the delay a user feels depends on how quickly text is emitted and on endpointing, the decision that the speaker has stopped \citep{shangguan2021latency}. The written form is usually produced after recognition: inverse text normalisation (ITN) turns spoken forms such as ``seven'' into ``7'' \citep{pusateri2017itn}, and disfluency removal turns a verbatim transcript into fluent text \citep{jamshidlou2020disfluency}. We score the output of these steps as the user receives it. Streaming systems also show partial text that may change before it is final; how often it changes can be measured \citep{shangguan2020stability}, but we score only the final text.

\paragraph{Running Whisper.} Whisper processes audio in 30-second windows, so live use needs extra steps. Whisper-Streaming re-runs the model on a growing buffer \citep{machacek2023whisperstreaming}, and WhisperX cuts long audio with a VAD before transcription \citep{bain2023whisperx}. Whisper can also write text that was never said, often around silence \citep{koenecke2024careless} and in noisy audio \citep{mansoor2025mitigating}. Section~\ref{sec:whisperguide} compares such choices for dictation.

\section{Systems and Settings}\label{app:systems}
We use each system's default settings, with the changes below. For Deepgram we turn on \texttt{punctuate} and \texttt{smart\_format}, which add punctuation and change how numbers, dates and similar items are written. GPT-Live has a \texttt{delay} setting that trades how early partial text appears against accuracy, and we found no documented default. We use \texttt{low}, first chosen on 50 of the English test clips.

\paragraph{GPT-Live's delay setting.} To check that choice, we ran \texttt{low} and \texttt{minimal} on the same day on every test set (Table~\ref{tab:gptdelay}). The typical wait for the final text is the same (744 and 752\,ms; slow case 899 and 882\,ms), and neither writes text on any no-speech clip. \texttt{minimal} has the higher WER on every English set, ours and the external ones, and on 9 of the 11 other language sets. Treating the 25 comparisons of the table as one group, the difference is clear (Holm-corrected) on quiet and whispered English, on both EARS sets and on three of the four VOiCES conditions, and of the other languages only on Hindi. It loses a language as often on EN\,+\,X recordings, and more often on X\,+\,Y with automatic detection (8.3\% against 5.0\%, also clear). The \texttt{low} runs of this check match those in the main tables to within 0.6 points on EARS and VOiCES; on our sets, Spanish (Puerto Rico) moved most (5.8\% in the main run, 3.1\% on 5 November), then Hindi (11.8\% and 14.0\%).

\paragraph{Other settings.} RT Whisper accepted only one language in our tests, so with two languages selected it is told neither. Whisper SH decodes with beam search (width 5); with two languages selected, it is given both as the allowed languages. It does no segmentation of its own, so the client cuts the audio into segments (Section~\ref{sec:whisperguide}). For ElevenLabs, the default settings mean the text is verbatim, including fillers such as ``uh'', and the text is finalised once, when the audio ends; Section~\ref{sec:cs} also tests finalising at each pause. For Zoom, we use the settings of its sample app, with text clean-up turned off. Each system is told the language a user would choose. If a system has no option for that language, we send none and the system detects the language itself. Zoom has no locale for Egypt, Latin America or Puerto Rico, so for those sets we use the closest one it has (Saudi Arabic; Spanish, Spain). It has no option for Urdu at all.

\paragraph{Regional language codes.} Systems that take a region with the language get one code per language in the main runs: Gemini \texttt{ar-EG} for every Arabic set and \texttt{es-US} for every Spanish set, and Zoom \texttt{ar-SA} and \texttt{es-ES}; the others take the bare language. On 5 November we ran each set again with the regional codes the providers document: Deepgram with \texttt{ar-EG}, \texttt{ar-SA}, \texttt{ar-AE} and \texttt{es-419}; Zoom with \texttt{ar-AE}, which its service accepted; and Gemini with \texttt{es-419} (its transcription documentation lists no Saudi or Emirati Arabic code). The transcripts were the same as in the main run on 78 of Deepgram's 80 clips, all 20 of Zoom's and 33 of Gemini's 40, and no failed clip changed. The largest change in WER was Deepgram on Spanish (Latin America), from 8.7\% to 7.8\%. So the dialect results do not come from the codes we sent.

\paragraph{End-of-turn and speech-detection checks.} On 5 November we ran the 16 whispered clips again with four changed setups, each against the system's main-run results: AAI 3.6 and AAI 3.5 sending \texttt{ForceEndpoint} before \texttt{Terminate}, so the turn in progress is finalised; the same with end-of-turn detection effectively off (\texttt{end\_of\_turn\_confidence\_threshold} 1, \texttt{max\_turn\_silence} 10\,s); Zoom with \texttt{silence\_duration\_ms} 5{,}000 instead of 600; and Qwen with our deployment's speech detection relaxed (\texttt{streaming\_vad\_config}: threshold 0.3, 2{,}000\,ms of silence, 300\,ms of padding), alongside a rerun with its default settings, which matched the main run (32.2\% of words missing in both). Section~\ref{sec:whisper} gives the results.

Each clip is sent in small chunks at the speed of speech, the way a microphone delivers it. Most systems receive 32\,ms chunks at 16\,kHz. Meta, GPT-Live and RT Whisper receive 32\,ms chunks at 24\,kHz, the rate their APIs expect, resampled from the 16\,kHz audio. The AAI models and Zoom receive 100\,ms chunks: AssemblyAI's API rejected chunks shorter than 50\,ms in our tests, and Zoom's sample app uses 100\,ms. When the clip ends, the client tells the system the audio is over and waits up to 30 seconds for the final text. Every clip uses a new session, and all systems were called from the same client machine.

To check that the systems did not change during the test, we replayed 42 clips to two hosted services (Gemini and Meta) and to the gated Whisper deployment (described in Section~\ref{sec:whisperguide}) one week after their first run. Whisper and Gemini returned the same text, and Meta's WER barely moved (16.5\% against 16.7\%, on the 41 clips it answered; one session was refused by a rate limit). The other systems were not rechecked.

\section{Data and Scoring Details}\label{app:data}
\paragraph{The spoken reference.} To build the spoken reference, we aligned the transcripts of the eleven systems' default (verbatim) settings with the script and proposed an edit wherever several systems heard the same departure (an added word when at least three did; a missing or changed word when at least five of eleven did, because on whispered speech four systems drop the same quiet words). Proposals with stronger agreement (at least four, or at least six) were shown already ticked. A member of the team then listened to every message, accepted or rejected each proposal and corrected the text by hand where needed (six messages). Complete words were kept as spoken, including words the reader then corrected; cut-off fragments and fillers (``um'', ``uh'') were left out, as they are not in the scripts either.

\paragraph{Correcting for many comparisons.} A difference is called clear only if its paired 95\% interval excludes zero and its two-sided paired-bootstrap p-value stays below 0.05 after a Holm correction within its group. The groups are: the lowest against the next-lowest system in each English condition; the four whispered missing-word shares against 3\%; the 13 name gaps; Deepgram's name gap against each other system's; script against spoken reference on quiet English, and the two clean-up settings against each other on the spoken reference; the two missing- and extra-word differences between Whisper SH and AAI 3.6; ElevenLabs NV against ElevenLabs on the Saudi and Emirati Arabic sets; gated Whisper with its VAD on and off; the Whisper setups on in-house whispered speech; English only against both languages selected, on all recordings; ElevenLabs finalising at each pause against once; the EARS changes from normal to whispered; the EARS Whisper setups; the VOiCES changes from the quiet far recording, with babble and with TV; and GPT-Live's two delay settings (Table~\ref{tab:gptdelay}). The scripts \texttt{paper/analysis/stats\_review.ts} (4{,}000 resamples) and \texttt{gptdelay.py} (2{,}000) compute them, and for the two-language tests the bootstrap resamples source clips (Section~\ref{sec:cs}). A difference shown only by its interval, outside these groups (for example the language averages and the name gaps on quiet English alone), is not called clear.

\paragraph{Normalisation.} Before comparing a transcript with the correct text, we ignore capital letters and punctuation. For Arabic and Urdu we remove short-vowel marks and the elongation character; for Arabic we also treat \textit{alif} with and without \textit{hamza} as equal, \textit{ta marbuta} as \textit{ha}, and \textit{alif maqsura} as \textit{ya}. We do not merge the Arabic and Urdu forms of \textit{yeh}, \textit{kaf} and \textit{heh}; no Urdu reference or transcript uses the Arabic forms, so this changes no score. Traditional and simplified Chinese characters are treated as equal.

\paragraph{The language sets.} Most are sentences read aloud (FLEURS, and the Puerto Rican Spanish set); the Arabic MSA (Egypt) set is Modern Standard Arabic read by Egyptian speakers, while the Saudi and Emirati sets are dialect speech, and the Spanish (Spain) set is European Parliament speech.

\paragraph{Mandarin.} Mandarin is not written with spaces, so we count each Chinese character, and each run of Latin letters or digits, as one unit: the mixed error rate (MER) used in Mandarin--English code-switching work \citep{lyu2010seame}, not the match error rate of \citet{morris2004wer}. We also compute the character error rate (CER), the same measure counted over characters; on our single-language Mandarin set MER equals CER. Chinese numerals in place of digits count as errors, as numbers do in every language.

\paragraph{Labelling names.} Each different word was then labelled as a name or not, following a written rule: part of the name of a person, organisation, product, service, programming language, place or titled work counts; days, months, time zones, titles such as ``Dr.'', job titles, acronyms such as ``API'' or ``PM'', document headings and ordinary words written with a capital do not. Only 156 of the 327 capitalised words are names, so the capital-letter rule alone is a poor way to find them. Adding the 22 occurrences of a listed name that the capital-letter rule misses (at the start of a sentence, or after ``Dr.'' or ``Mr.'') and the 5 lower-case uses of a listed product name gives 183 name words (156 + 22 + 5).

\section{Accent Labels}\label{app:accent}
We labelled each in-house recording with CommonAccent \citep{zuluagagomez2023commonaccent}, an English accent classifier with 16 classes trained on Common Voice, over 4-second windows taken every 2 seconds, keeping windows whose top class has a probability of at least 0.7. On the 90 spoken messages (quiet and fan on), 62\% of these windows are labelled US English and 29\% South Asian English (the classifier's Indian English class); England, New Zealand and Ireland together make up 7\%, and every other class under 1\%. South Asian English appears in 64 of the 90 messages but is the label for the whole message in only 18. Of consecutive windows, 28\% change label, against 4\% on the 428 normal-voice EARS clips, whose 107 speakers each keep one accent; we take the EARS rate as the classifier's own noise. The reader confirmed that the US, South Asian, British and Irish stretches were deliberate. On whispered messages the classifier labels 98\% of windows US English and changes label no more often than on EARS, so it finds no accent cue in whispered speech. Messages labelled mostly South Asian English (25 of the 90) have about the same WER as the rest for every system in Table~\ref{tab:overall}: no difference is clearly outside chance in a bootstrap over messages. But 16 of the 25 are the fan-on messages, so accent and condition cannot be separated.

\paragraph{Number habits and normalised scores.} These switches are part of the WER differences in Table~\ref{tab:overall}, and a benchmark that converts numbers to a common form does not measure them. To see how much they matter, Table~\ref{tab:normwer} re-scores English after applying Whisper's English text normaliser \citep{radford2023whisper} to both the reference and the transcript. The normaliser writes numbers as digits, standardises contractions and spellings, and removes fillers such as ``uh''. The normalised scores also split text into words slightly differently, so we compare them with the raw WER under the same word splitting. On quiet English every WER falls, by 1.0--3.8 points. The systems that write digits as words or keep fillers gain the most: Qwen (3.8 points), ElevenLabs (3.5), Deepgram (2.5), Meta (2.2), and GPT-Live and AAI 3.5 (2.1 and 1.6). The order changes little (Spearman rank correlation 0.98), and Gemini Smart stays lowest on quiet English. An app that converts numbers after recognition would remove part of this difference; we did not test this.

\paragraph{Gemini Smart against Gemini.} Smart lowers Gemini's quiet-English WER from 6.9\% to 3.9\%. Almost all of the difference is in extra words, which fall from 3.7\% to 0.7\% of words. With the fan on (3.2\% against 2.5\%) and whispered speech (4.2\% against 5.0\%) the two settings are close. When capital letters and punctuation are also scored, Smart is worse with the fan on (10.0\% against 6.4\%) and whispered speech (10.9\% against 8.6\%). In the other languages, the largest changes are Urdu, where WER falls from 51.8\% to 32.4\% (Section~\ref{sec:script}), and Saudi Arabic, where it rises from 29.3\% to 35.2\%.

\paragraph{ElevenLabs NV against ElevenLabs.} Without verbatim output, ElevenLabs' quiet-English WER falls from 12.8\% to 5.1\%, and its extra words from 8.1\% to 1.4\% of words. With the fan on (4.5\% against 5.8\%) and on whispered speech (7.1\% against 9.1\%) it also improves. The Saudi and Emirati Arabic sets get clearly worse: Saudi Arabic rises from 34.8\% to 66.0\% (paired difference 31.3 points, 95\% CI 21.5 to 40.2) and Emirati Arabic from 61.8\% to 79.4\% (17.6 points, 95\% CI 9.1 to 25.9), while Arabic MSA (Egypt) and the other languages change by less than 3 points (Table~\ref{tab:fworst} gives its failed clips).

\paragraph{Ranks against the two references.} Apart from the top of the quiet column, the order of the systems changes little: over the thirteen rows of Table~\ref{tab:verbatim}, the Spearman rank correlation between the two columns is 0.93 on quiet English, 0.78 with the fan on and 0.98 on whispered speech.

\paragraph{Clips hard for one system only.} Across all 326 speech clips, 23 are above 30\% for exactly one system: 9 for Qwen, 6 for Deepgram, 3 each for Zoom and ElevenLabs, and 2 for Whisper SH (both Spanish (Spain), where it replaced the speech with a stock phrase; Section~\ref{sec:whisperguide}).

\paragraph{Character error rates on the Arabic dialects.} Character error rates are far below the word error rates (11--27\% on Saudi and 15--27\% on Emirati Arabic with default settings; ElevenLabs NV 41\% and 51\%), which is consistent with spelling variation but does not show it: Arabic words carry attached prefixes, so CER is far below WER on Arabic MSA (Egypt) too (0.5--4.3\% against 2.6--14.3\%).

\paragraph{Hindi.} AAI 3.5 fails on 25\% of Hindi clips, and Whisper SH and Zoom on 20\% each. Gemini fails on none, and has the lowest Hindi WER in both settings (3.1\%, and 2.6\% with Smart). Zoom has the highest Hindi WER of the eleven systems (34.6\%). Its text is in the right writing system, but its character error rate (16.3\%) is less than half its WER, so many of its wrong words are near-misses at the character level rather than different words (CER counts Unicode characters, so a vowel sign counts separately). The same holds for Whisper SH (13.6\% against 29.8\%), and almost for AAI 3.5 (13.0\% against 25.9\%), but not for Meta or Deepgram, whose character and word error rates are about equal. Merging common Devanagari spelling variants (the nukta, and chandrabindu with anusvara) lowers Hindi WER by at most 2.2 points for any system (Zoom: 34.6\% to 33.3\%), so these variants do not explain the gap.

\subsection{Speed}\label{app:speed}
Table~\ref{tab:latency} gives two delays, measured on the test client. The \emph{wait} is the time from the client's end-of-audio signal to the final text (the final hypothesis), the delay after the speaker stops. Because the client signals the end, the wait does not include endpointing, the time a system would take to decide by itself that the speaker has stopped. The wait ends at the signal each service gives that it has nothing more to send, which differs between services: the final text itself for Meta, Gemini, ElevenLabs, GPT-Live and RT Whisper; the end-of-session message for AAI and Zoom; the closing of the connection for Deepgram; and an end-of-audio message from our own deployments (Whisper SH, gated Whisper and Qwen). For the services that end with a session message, the wait can include a short time after the last text arrived. Runs used up to six sessions at a time per system. The \emph{connect} time is how long it takes to open a session, which an app could hide by connecting early. The table gives the typical value (the median, p50) and a slow case (p90: 90\% of sessions were faster than this). From our client location, Meta, Deepgram, Whisper SH, Qwen and both ElevenLabs settings have typical waits under 400\,ms; GPT-Live and RT Whisper wait about 750\,ms, and the AAI models have the slowest p90, over 1{,}200\,ms. Gemini (584\,ms) and Gemini Smart (434\,ms) were run on different days; side by side on the same 50 English clips, twice, their typical waits differed by only 10\,ms. Only Gemini's wait grows with the length of the clip: its typical wait is 591\,ms on English clips under 20 seconds and 1{,}084\,ms on clips of a minute or more (442\,ms and 951\,ms for Smart). For every other system it changes by less than 100\,ms across clip lengths. A repeat run on 29 October also recorded when text was first finalised during speech and the network round trip to each provider (Appendix~\ref{app:extra}, Table~\ref{tab:timing}); there, waits moved by up to 320\,ms, so we treat them as indicative.

\paragraph{Text during speech, and the network.} The wait in Table~\ref{tab:latency} is what a user feels after they stop. A second question is whether any text is final (a final hypothesis, as opposed to partial text) while they are still speaking. On 29 October we played the 106 English messages to every system again, recording when the first finalised text arrived and, during the same runs, the round trip from the test client to each provider (Table~\ref{tab:timing}). Whisper SH, Qwen, Deepgram, Zoom and the AAI models finalise text during speech on 83--99\% of messages, typically 5--9 seconds in. Meta, Gemini, GPT-Live and RT Whisper finalise only at the end, as set up (Appendix~\ref{app:systems}). ElevenLabs, though set to finalise once, finalised the first 36 seconds early on every message longer than about 35 seconds, and on no shorter message. Partial text was not measured. The round trip explains part of the wait: subtracting it moves Deepgram from seventh to third, but the same six rows stay slowest (both AAI models, Gemini in both settings, GPT-Live and RT Whisper), at 594--716\,ms beyond the round trip. Waits on 29 October differed from the main run by up to 165\,ms for most systems and 320\,ms for Gemini Smart.
