\paragraph{Gemini under repeated and parallel use.} Because Gemini's wait changed from one day to the next, we ran two more tests on 21 October. In the first, three English clips (10, 45 and 91 seconds long) were played to Gemini and Gemini Smart at the same moment, 20 times each. Across the 60 pairs, Smart's typical wait was 17\,ms shorter (it was faster in 42 of 60 pairs), and each setting returned the same text in every round that day. The wait grew with the length of the clip: about 450--500\,ms for the 10-second clip and 1{,}040--1{,}090\,ms for the 91-second one. In the second test, we kept up to 50 sessions open at once. No session failed. The typical wait stayed between 510 and 640\,ms, while the slow case grew at 25 and 50 open sessions (to 910\,ms for Gemini at 25, and 1{,}080\,ms for Gemini Smart at 50). We repeated both tests on 22 October. Up to 25 open sessions, typical waits were again 575--630\,ms; but at 50, Gemini's typical wait rose to 1{,}369\,ms (slow case 3{,}587\,ms) and Gemini Smart's to 697\,ms (1{,}255\,ms). In the repeated pairs, Smart was faster in 33 of 60, against 42 of 60 the day before, and each setting returned the same text in 90--100\% of rounds rather than every round. Waits under load therefore varied from day to day.

\section{EARS and VOiCES: Details}\label{app:ext}
\paragraph{The EARS speakers.} The 107 EARS speakers are 60 women, 43 men and 4 other or not stated, aged 18 to 75, mostly native speakers of American English. On whispered speech Whisper SH loses 10.4\% of words as missing words, against 7.3\% for each AAI model, where on our speaker it lost far fewer; the intervals of the three changes overlap, so this difference is within chance.

\paragraph{The VOiCES clips.} We take 100 sentences, one per speaker (50 women, 50 men), each in four versions: the original clean recording, and the room recording from one studio microphone at the far position in room 4 with no background sound, with babble (several people talking) and with a television playing. That is 400 clips, 26 minutes per version.

\paragraph{Scoring.} The VOiCES references are LibriSpeech text: lower case, no punctuation and numbers as words. So for both corpora we apply Whisper's English text normaliser to the reference and the transcript, as in Table~\ref{tab:normwer}, and report only WER. Two kinds of clip have no text and count as empty transcripts: clips that gated Whisper's VAD never sent, and sessions with no transcript within 30 seconds. Only Gemini had the second kind, all on noisy clips. In the one session we traced, on a babble clip, the connection stayed open and Gemini returned ``Add, and,'' for a 15.8-second sentence, 17 seconds after the audio ended; we did not trace the others, so some may have other causes. Intervals resample speakers.

\paragraph{Distance and noise.} On the clean recordings every system is between 2.1\% and 4.6\%. A far microphone in a quiet room adds little for most: under 3 points for Whisper SH, Gemini (in both settings), the AAI models and ElevenLabs (in both settings), 4--6 points for Meta, Deepgram, GPT-Live, RT Whisper and Zoom, and 8--10 for Qwen and gated Whisper. With babble, WER rises for every system to between 38.7\% (Zoom) and 94.9\% (Deepgram), 31--85 points above the quiet far recording. For eleven of the fourteen rows (the thirteen rows and gated Whisper) the errors are mostly missing words, which may come from the service's own speech detection as well as from recognition; Qwen and ElevenLabs (in both settings) write more wrong words than they miss. Extra words are at most 7.3\%, so no system writes down much of the background talk. Gemini returned no text within 30 seconds on 67 of the 100 babble clips and 7 of the television clips, and Gemini Smart on 12 babble clips; these count as empty transcripts, so most of Gemini's babble WER is these sessions. With a television, WER rises less and differs more between systems: Zoom rises by 2.6 points (95\% CI $-0.4$ to 5.8, within chance) and the AAI models by 7.4--8.3, while Deepgram rises by 40 and RT Whisper by 32. Zoom shows that the quiet far-microphone results do not predict the noisy ones: it is worse than average with a far microphone in a quiet room, but lowest with babble and with television. Left out of the WER, Gemini's 67 babble sessions with no text leave a WER of 40.3\% on the other 33 clips, and Gemini Smart's 12 leave 67.1\%; these are only the easier clips, so they are lower bounds.

\paragraph{ElevenLabs and finalising.} By default, ElevenLabs finalises each recording once, at the end, and loses the non-English part even of Spanish recordings that it transcribes when played alone, rarely writing anything in its place. We ran the test again on 29 October, on the screened recordings, with ElevenLabs set to finalise at each pause of 300\,ms. This matches the 300\,ms gap we put between the two clips, so switches without such a pause may behave differently, and the two runs are about two weeks apart. With both languages selected, recordings with a missing language fell from 61\% to 1\% with English (1 of 85; 95\% CI 0 to 7\%) and from 92\% to 36\% without (95\% CI 26 to 47\%); for ElevenLabs NV, from 80\% to 2\% and from 96\% to 62\%. Without English, the part still lost is almost always the second (80 of 83 recordings with both languages selected).

With both languages selected, systems that accept several languages are given both. Deepgram uses its multi-language mode for both settings; its documentation lists that mode for English, Spanish, French, German, Hindi, Russian, Portuguese, Japanese, Italian and Dutch \citep{deepgramdocs}, so Arabic and Mandarin are outside it. RT Whisper is given no language in either setting, and Zoom, which takes one language, is given none and uses its default, which behaves like English. So for these three, the both-languages and automatic settings send the same request. Deepgram's and Zoom's gave the same result on every recording; RT Whisper's differed on 1 of the 85 recordings with English and 2 of the 232 without. Qwen is sent both languages as \texttt{language\_options} with both selected, and no language with automatic detection, but it wrote the same text in the two settings on all 400 recordings.

\section{Running Whisper: Further Results}\label{app:whisper}
\paragraph{Cutting at pauses, in full.} Turning the gated deployment's VAD off is not enough: that deployment still has a whispered WER of 61.1\%, almost all of it missing words (50\% of words), and in 44\% of whispered clips it drops 5 or more words from the last third. The self-hosted deployment, which transcribes exactly the segments the client cuts, loses almost nothing on the same clips (1.8\% missing words, no cut-off endings). The two are different deployments, and the gated deployment's server still runs its own speech detection, so this comparison does not isolate the cutting rule from that second detector; we have not measured where that server cuts its segments or what it drops. On EARS the pattern repeats: with its VAD off, the gated deployment still loses 30.5\% of whispered words, against 10.4\% for the self-hosted deployment (Table~\ref{tab:earsvad}). Cutting at the speaker's own pauses is also as fast as the gated setup: 361\,ms typical wait against 360\,ms, with a shorter slow case (498\,ms against 596\,ms).

\paragraph{Invented text, in full.} Because of the two stock phrases (Section~\ref{sec:whisperguide}, Finding 4), the self-hosted deployment's WER on Spanish (Spain) is 19.5\%, about twice the gated setup's 10.0\%. A VAD that decides only whether to send a segment at all prevents text on silence: Whisper-1 split wrote nothing on any no-speech clip. But the same rule cost it the whispered clips the VAD did not hear (23.4\% against 7.7\% for Whisper-1), so a VAD should not be allowed to skip segments that may contain quiet speech.

\paragraph{The nine setups in full.}
\begin{enumerate}\itemsep1pt
  \item \textbf{Gated, VAD on (``gated Whisper'').} A deployment on Baseten with a voice gate on the client: a Silero VAD in front of Whisper drops audio it judges to be silence: it waits for speech above a 0.5 probability, keeps 96\,ms before it, sends at most 512\,ms of any pause, and stops sending after 544\,ms of silence. The deployment cuts the audio into segments itself, with its own server-side speech detection, which we do not control.
  \item \textbf{Gated, VAD off.} The same deployment, sent all of the audio: the client's Silero VAD is off, but the server's own speech detection still runs.
  \item \textbf{Self-hosted, Silero cuts (``Whisper SH'').} A second deployment of our own, which does no segmentation. The client runs the same VAD only to decide where each segment ends: at a pause of 544\,ms after speech, once at least 5 seconds have been sent, and always before 30 seconds. It then tells the server to transcribe that segment. Every sample of audio is sent.
  \item \textbf{Self-hosted, Silero drops.} The same deployment, with Silero VAD also dropping audio as in setup 1.
  \item \textbf{Self-hosted, TEN cuts.} Setup 3 with TEN VAD \citep{tenvad}, an open VAD from the TEN framework, in place of Silero, at its default threshold of 0.5. Every sample is sent.
  \item \textbf{Self-hosted, TEN drops.} Setup 4 with TEN VAD: the same rules decide which audio is dropped, using TEN's speech probabilities instead of Silero's.
  \item \textbf{OpenAI GPT-Realtime-Whisper (``RT Whisper'').} OpenAI's hosted streaming Whisper.
  \item \textbf{OpenAI Whisper-1.} OpenAI's file transcription, so the whole recording is uploaded when the user stops.
  \item \textbf{Whisper-1 split.} Whisper-1 with the client cutting the recording at pauses, using the VAD rule of setup 3, and uploading each segment as soon as it is cut, with the previous segment's text as context. A segment in which the VAD heard no speech is not sent.
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{TEN VAD, further results.} On EARS, TEN also gives slightly lower WER than Silero when only cutting (9.5\% against 11.5\%, 95\% CI of the difference $-3.7$ to $-0.3$). The reason is the one given in Section~\ref{sec:whisperguide}: TEN calls far more of the whispered audio speech than Silero does. On the no-speech clips, both call almost nothing speech at 0.5 (0.4\% and 0\%). Dropping with TEN also gives the self-hosted deployment a quiet-English WER of 7.2\% (against 8.3\% when sending all of the audio, within its interval) and an other-language average of 17.6\%, lowers Spanish (Spain) from 19.5\% to 14.7\% (one clip that came back as ``Gracias, se\~nor presidente.'' is now transcribed correctly, though the other stock phrases remain), and reduces the no-speech clips with text from 6 to 2. The cost is a slightly longer wait (395\,ms against 361\,ms typical) and more lost languages in two-language recordings (54\% against 45\% with English, 96\% against 87\% without, with both languages selected), as with Silero dropping.

\paragraph{The threshold sweep.} To check whether the Silero result is only a matter of its threshold, we repeated both dropping setups with the drop threshold at 0.2, 0.3 and 0.4, on the whispered, fan-on and no-speech clips (Figure~\ref{fig:vadsweep}). Lowering Silero's threshold helps only a little: whispered WER falls from 51.4\% at 0.5 to 41.1\% at 0.2, still four times the 10.1\% of sending all of the audio, because even at 0.2 Silero calls only 52\% of the whispered audio speech. TEN keeps whispered WER between 10.0\% and 10.7\% at every threshold. Neither VAD's fan-on WER moves by more than 2.1 points, and the no-speech clips with text stay at 0 of 10 for Silero and 2 of 10 for TEN at every threshold.

\section{Further Limitations}\label{app:limits}
The spoken references were drafted from the tested systems' own transcripts and confirmed by one listener, a member of the team, so a departure that no system heard, or that the listener missed, stays as in the script. Most analyses use the script, which favours the clean-up settings on extra words. Accents were labelled by a classifier trained on natural accents, not on accents a speaker puts on; we checked its labels only against the reader's own account. Names were labelled by a language model (Claude) following the written rule of Section~\ref{sec:names}, not by a person, and a listed word counts as a name wherever it appears in a message, so 5 of the 183 are lower-case uses of a product name. The spoken reference removes fillers (``um'', ``uh''), as the scripts do, so it is a record of the words said, not a full verbatim transcript. Romanised and translated parts are detected by rule, only when the two languages use different writing systems, and were checked by hand only on a few examples. The two-language recordings switch speaker and recording source along with the language, and the screened recordings of Appendix~\ref{app:cs} were chosen using the tested systems themselves. The analysis thresholds (Table~\ref{tab:taxonomy}) are rules of thumb; other thresholds would change the counts.

Some choices were made on the test data: the two Whisper setups in the main comparison were chosen after the comparison in Section~\ref{sec:whisperguide}. GPT-Live's \texttt{delay} setting was first chosen on 50 of the English test clips; Table~\ref{tab:gptdelay} now reports both settings on every test set.

Some systems and settings were not fully tested. Gated Whisper's two-language runs used its VAD. ElevenLabs was tested with its default settings and with \texttt{no\_verbatim}; finalising at each pause was tested only on the two-language recordings. Other settings may change the results, as the Gemini Smart and ElevenLabs NV rows show. Zoom used the settings of its sample app. Whisper SH's segment cutting, and its use of TEN VAD, were implemented in our test client. The threshold sweep covered only the dropping setups, on the whispered, fan-on and no-speech clips, with one run per threshold, and only with the self-hosted deployment. Systems were tested on different days (Appendix~\ref{app:systems}).

Each clip was played once per system and setting, except where stated, so we do not measure how much results vary between runs, apart from the one-week check in Appendix~\ref{app:systems} and the repeated Gemini tests. All waits were measured from one client location, and the network round trip to each service differs (Table~\ref{tab:timing}), so the waits are indicative rather than a ranking; repeated 9 to 28 days later, the median waits moved by up to 320\,ms. Results for hosted services reflect their versions at the time of testing; the released transcripts record what each system returned then, but a rerun today may differ.
